data.title: Keyboard-Locale Punctuation Tells in Claimed-Local Content
data.summary:
Content attributed to a persona or outlet claiming one linguistic origin carries
punctuation and input habits specific to a different keyboard layout or locale,
contradicting the claimed authorship.
data.description:
Typography is a habit, not a choice an author reconsiders sentence by sentence, and
habits formed on one keyboard survive a change of language. The clearest example in this
corpus is a space inserted before a closing `?`, `!`, `:` or `;` — "word ? Word" rather
than "word? Word". English typography has no such space; French does, as a typographic
convention tied to the AZERTY layout and to the locale of the word processor or
translation tool that produced the text. Text in English or any other language that
carries this spacing consistently was produced by, or through tooling configured for, a
French-locale input chain.

The same family of tell includes a decimal comma where the claimed locale uses a point, a
non-breaking space before a percent or currency sign, a dd/mm date where the audience
reads mm/dd, and curly quotation marks of a style the claimed publishing platform does not
emit natively. None of these are proof on their own — a single instance is a typo, a
pasted quotation, or a style guide nobody enforced. The signal is in the pattern: the same
tell recurring across unrelated articles, accounts or personas that are not supposed to
share an author.

The tell points at the production chain — an operator, a translation tool, a shared
template, an outsourced content vendor — rather than directly at an individual or a
nationality, and it says nothing about who tasked the chain. Treat it as one input to the
report's attribution hypotheses, weighed alongside infrastructure and behavioural
indicators, not as a conclusion that stands alone.
data.recommendation:
* Catalogue every typographic tell across the corpus — punctuation spacing, decimal and
  date format, quotation style — before citing any of it; a pattern claim needs the count
  behind it.
* Treat a tell as signal only where it recurs across content that is not supposed to
  share an author or a production chain; a single instance stays a typo.
* Feed the finding into the attribution section's competing hypotheses alongside
  infrastructure and behavioural indicators, rather than naming an origin from typography
  alone.
* Hold back the exact catalogue of tells from anything published; it is a checklist for
  the next revision's proofreader.
data.short_recommendation: Catalogue recurring typographic tells and weigh them only alongside other indicators.
